headline: EPA scraps limits on power plant pollution
summary: The EPA is repealing most of the Biden-era rules that limited greenhouse gases from coal and gas power plants. Its head, Lee Zeldin, says the change will save $310 billion and lower energy prices. The agency also wants to drop every remaining greenhouse gas rule for power plants. Power plants make about a quarter of US emissions.

cover_question.q: Why drop a rule that cuts pollution?

cover_answer: The EPA says it cost too much and went past its power.
table_question: If a rule costs a lot but might save lives, do you keep it?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: Power plants burn coal and gas to make electricity, and gases go up into the air. Those gases wrap the Earth like a blanket and warm it up. There was a rule to make big plants put out less. The government took that rule away yesterday. Our lights still work, and the grown-ups are arguing about it.
5-7.why: Electricity and a blanket are things they can touch. They don't need the politics.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: Coal and gas plants make about a quarter of the heat-trapping gases the US puts out. A 2024 rule told them to cut way down. The EPA erased it Monday, saying it cost too much and demanded unproven technology. Like a thermostat with the limit switched off.

13-17.script: Is $310 billion too much for a rule projected to prevent 4,500 early deaths a year? Those are the two sides' numbers for the power plant limits the EPA repealed. The EPA says the harm is too uncertain to pin on plants. Who has to prove what?
13-17.why: Two numbers, two sides. Teens can weigh them.

5-7.a: A part of the government that makes rules about clean air and water. This week it took a rule away.

8-12.q: How does a power plant change the weather?
8-12.a: Burning coal and gas puts carbon dioxide in the air, and that traps heat. Power plants make about a quarter of the US total.

8-12.q: Who decides the rules for pollution?
8-12.a: The EPA, under the Clean Air Act. One president's EPA wrote these rules. The next one is erasing them.

13-17.q: Why drop a rule that cuts pollution?
13-17.a: The EPA says it cost too much, and the law didn't let it demand technology plants can't use yet. Critics call it a giant step backward.

13-17.q: Will this actually change the climate?
13-17.a: Unclear. Coal has been shrinking because solar and other clean power got cheap. One study says rollbacks slow emissions cuts but don't reverse them.
